rv.q: And what a joyous, sad, beautiful piece it is — muscular, vibrant, deeply tender.

With six guys in an encounter group set up on a multi-coloured stage fitted with stacking chairs and scaffolding, Ryan Calais Cameron's play works through some of the stigmatising social obstacles faced by young black men with disarming honesty and humour.
Cameron’s production is its own fresh and startling thing.
Every single performance is a stand-out.
Lyrical new play For Black Boys Who Have When the Hue Gets Too Heavy lives up to its weighty name.
It's worth a thousand sociology reports compiled by right-on think tanks. And it's fun.
Calais Cameron's show is rewardingly stuffed with comic asides and digressions.
This play with songs and dance moves works hard and successfully to lift audience spirits by making trauma palatable as well as distressing.

cn.t: Critics hail this meditation on Black masculinity as beautiful, joyous, and deeply tender, praising its lyrical writing, natural performances, and fresh theatrical vocabulary that addresses mental health with disarming honesty and grace.
